item.title: Ask HN: Internal AI Language
item.description:
LLMs have an internal language that they translate English into before predicting the next token. Like 'king' is translated into a word of an internal language that corresponds to vector [monarch, man], which allows king-man+woman=queen. Spanish is similar for the case 'queen'=reina, - ina suffix means female, but becomes irregular for king=rey.

We have tried to create regular, consistent languages (loglan, lojban, ithkuil), and there seems to be one in the first layers of LLMs, derived from all text ever written. This internal language is currently expressed as vectors, but we could devise a lexicon to map them, and if we could learn it we could communicate more directly with machines, dispensing with some layers and getting rid of language ambiguities.

Makes sense? Is someone working on this?

It's like Arrival but with AI instead of aliens.

item.title: Show HN: Higherlevel – Define and review what AI agents build
item.description:
Hi HN!

I'm Ryan, I'm building Higherlevel (https://higherlevel.to) so product teams have one place to define and review software changes.

Over the last couple of years, I've been increasingly delegating software implementation to AI coding agents.

However, because it became easier and faster to ship complexity, I realised that it still takes me quite some time to even understand what the software is doing, why it is doing that, or review the changes.

I also don't do traditional code reviews anymore, it's mostly automated but I still want to review the final outcome of the changes (rather than its implementation).

I regularly work on complex B2B applications where a single feature can involve dozen of business rules, edge cases and interactions with existing functionality.

I found myself spending more and more time discovering and explaining requirements to agents, reviewing their output, asking for evdience and trying to establish whether we actually agreed on what correct behaviour looked like.

So I built Higherlevel. The idea is to bring product specifications and proof of work into a single collaborative workspace.

You can: - describe the current behaviour, known limitations and expected changes - define business rules, acceptance scenarios using Given/When/Then - demand evidence in the form of a screenshot, a video, etc - comment directly on the spec, on a specific area of the image or a timestamp of the video - discuss changes, track revisions and approve results with your team

I've written extensively about why I believe in specification driven development (and what it means to me) here https://higherlevel.to/blog/introducing-higherlevel

Higherlevel is currently in beta and built with Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, and PostgreSQL.

item.title: We gave an AI a phone and asked 1000 SF businesses a question
item.description:
We ran an experiment for SF Tech Week trying to understand how SF businesses are ready for AI. Very soon, every personal assistant like Muse, Instinct, Dots is going to call local places for us, so we wanted to understand what happens.

Our AI called the businesses across different categories - vets, bars, cafes, dentists, hair salons etc. It was introducing itself as AI on every call and then asked a question which fits the business like “Are you taking new patients” for dental places. We called only during business hours.

What we found: - Only 1 out of 3 businesses kept talking after picking the phone - Vets were 79%, dentists 61%, bars and dry cleaners - around 20% - Most people did not argue, but silently hung up after listening to the intro - 1 out 25 businesses already had AI reception answering the phone

Caveats - it is just one city and one week, so small differences between neighbourhoods could be a noise.

We would really love to hear how you are handling this if you are building AI voice agents calling places for people
